description: Josef K. is arrested one morning without knowing why. Kafka describes an endless process, an opaque bureaucracy: the word “Kafkaesque” was born from this nightmare.

hero.hook: Arrested without a crime, judged without understanding: the novel that invented the word “Kafkaesque”.

blocks.text: Written between **1914** and **1915**, published posthumously in **1925**, **Tea** Trial of **Franz Kafka** is one of the most influential works of the 20th century. **Josef K.**, a bank employee in Prague, is arrested one morning without being explained why. He struggles in an opaque legal system, with no visible rules or possible end.

Today, the adjective  designates the bureaucratic absurdity which crushes the individual without recourse. Kafka captures modern anxiety in the face of anonymous structures on which we depend without ever understanding them. His novel remains strangely current in the era of algorithms and inscrutable administrations. **[[The Kafkaesque]]**

Kafka leads a double life: insurance official in **Prague** by day, writer by night. A Jew of **German-speaking** culture in , he feels marginalized at the heart of an empire which collapsed after the First World War. **[[Austro-Hungarian Empire]]**

blocks.caption: Franz Kafka, between daytime bureaucracy and nighttime writing.

blocks.text: Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts. Brod refused and published The Trial in 1925, sometimes guessing the order of the chapters.

The unfinished novel paradoxically reinforces its power: the reader, like Josef K., cannot close the case or grasp an overall logic. The incomplete becomes part of the meaning. Kafka knows intimately the bureaucracy he denounces, since he was a model employee.

sections.title: Kafka: the man at the service of the unfinished

blocks.text: “Someone must have slandered Josef K., because, without having done anything wrong, he was arrested one morning. » K. remains free to move, but this apparent freedom becomes a permanent torment. He runs after lawyers, painters, intermediaries, without ever understanding the accusation or the hierarchy of the court.

blocks.caption: Prague at the beginning of the 20th century: setting of an empire and an opaque bureaucracy.

blocks.text: The courts sit in the attics of popular buildings, far from the official palaces. The system does not seek to prove guilt with evidence: it waits for the accused to exhaust themselves in endless procedures. The more K. defends himself, the more he validates an authority that does not really listen to him.

sections.title: Josef K. and the spiral of invisible accusation

blocks.text: Kafka criticizes **modern bureaucracy**, a machine so complex that no individual sees its entire functioning. Irony of history: Kafka was a model employee, promoter of safety helmets for workers in his insurance administration.

We can also read the trial as a : K. would not be guilty of any specific crime, but of the very state of being human, imperfect and vulnerable. In the cathedral, a priest recounts the , where a man waits his whole life in front of a closed door, without ever daring to cross it. **[[Existential guilt]]** **[[Parable of the Law]]**
Someone must have slandered Josef K., because, without having done anything wrong, he was arrested one morning.

The word  goes beyond literature. He describes the anxiety born from an opaque system: administrations, algorithms, corporate hierarchies, procedures without an identifiable interlocutor. The individual depends on a machine that he does not understand and cannot challenge effectively. **[[The Kafkaesque]]**

**Sartre**, **Camus** and **existentialism** recognize Kafka as a precursor. Josef K. was executed while whispering “Like a dog!” ". The novel refuses any reassuring conclusion: it forces the reader to live in uncertainty.
**The Trial** shows that one can be convicted without a crime or a fair trial. Kafka invents a language to name modern fear in the face of faceless power.
